Unlike the singular forms, the plural forms are mostly antiquated terms of formal address in the modern language, and second person plural pronouns are almost always used instead.

      Norwegian Bokmål

      Pronunciation

      • IPA(key): /ʋiː/, [ʋiː]
      • Audio:(file)
      • Rhymes: -iː
      • Homophones: hvi, vid
      • Hyphenation: vi

      Etymology 1

      PIE word
      *wéy

      Inherited from Middle Norwegian wi (“we”), attested in a Norwegian charter from 1415.[1] NAOB dates the form's appearance in Norwegian to about 1370 and considers it probably introduced from Old Danish wi and Old Swedish vī, vīr, corresponding to Old Norse vér.[2]

      On this account, the East Scandinavian forms continue Proto-Germanic *wīz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wéy (“we”). Bokmålsordboka more cautiously describes Swedish and Danish influence and also compares the Old Norse dual vit (“we two”), alongside the plural vér.[3]

      Compare Danish vi, Swedish vi, Icelandic vér, Gothic 𐍅𐌴𐌹𐍃 (weis), Dutch wij, German wir and English we (“we”).

      Pronoun

      vi

      1. we; the speaker together with one or more other people
        Vi kommer i morgen. ― We are coming tomorrow.
        • 1838, Henrik Wergeland, “Det første Haandtryk”, in Herman Jæger, editor, Samlede Skrifter: trykt og utrykt‎, volume I,2, published 1919, page 188:
          Din Puls har banket min imod.
          Forente var vi Blod i Blod.
          Your pulse has beaten against mine.
          United, we were blood within blood.
        • 1857, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, “Synnøves Sang”, in Francis Bull, editor, Samlede Digte‎, volume I, published 1926, page 27:
          nu tak for alt ifra vi var smaa
          Now, thank you for everything since we were little.
        • 1884, Henrik Ibsen, Vildanden‎, page 152:
          du og jeg, Hedvig, – vi to
          You and I, Hedvig—the two of us.
        • 1936, Sfinx, Kjent folk gjennem årene‎, page 14:
          hvis atte mor ikke hadde giftet sig med far, hadde vi vært oss da?
          If Mum hadn't married Dad, would we have been us then?
        • 2005, Inge Eidsvåg, Den gode lærer i liv og diktning‎:
          vi satte oss ned og begynte samtalen
          We sat down and began the conversation.
        • 2010, Ørnulf Hodne, Folkeskolen i folkeminnet:
          vi tre, Ole, Svein og jeg
          The three of us, Ole, Svein and I.
      2. we; a community, institution, nation or other group with which the speaker identifies or on whose behalf the speaker acts
        Vi takker for henvendelsen og svarer så snart som mulig. ― We thank you for your enquiry and will reply as soon as possible.
        • traditional, 1 Kor [First Corinthians]‎, 2011 edition, Bibelselskapet, 12:13:
          For med én Ånd ble vi alle døpt til å være én kropp
          For in one Spirit we were all baptized to be one body.
        • 1841, Henrik Wergeland, “Smaaguttenes Nationalsang”, in Herman Jæger, editor, Samlede Skrifter: trykt og utrykt‎, volume I,2, published 1919, page 406:
          Vi ere en Nation vi med,
          vi Smaa, en Alen lange:
          We are a nation too,
          we little ones, an ell tall.
        • 1859, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, “Ja, vi elsker dette landet”, in Francis Bull, editor, Samlede Digte‎, volume I, published 1926, page 45:
          ja, vi elsker dette landet
          Yes, we love this country.
        • 1863, Henrik Ibsen, Kongs-Emnerne‎, published 1872, page 192:
          vi væbner os det bedste vi kan
          We arm ourselves as best we can.
        • 1867, Henrik Ibsen, Peer Gynt‎, published 1874, page 127:
          vi mænd fra nord forstår at føre vor krig igjennem
          We men from the north know how to carry our war through.
        • 1869, Henrik Ibsen, De unges forbund‎, published 1874, page 51:
          hele herligheden faldt i fisk, som vi siger i trykkeriet
          The whole thing came to nothing, as we say at the printing house.
        • 1874, Henrik Ibsen, Fru Inger til Østråt‎, page 175:
          vi voksne har ikke noget med vor barnetro at skaffe
          We adults have nothing to do with our childhood faith.
        • 1875, Henrik Ibsen, “I en komponists stambog”, in Digte‎, page 177:
          stene har vort Norge nok af; vilddyr har vi og en flok af
          Our Norway has plenty of stones; we also have a pack of wild beasts.
        • 1880, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, “Salme II”, in Francis Bull, editor, Samlede Digte‎, volume II, published 1926, page 138:
          evigheds afkom og frø er vi alle
          We are all eternity's offspring and seed.
        • 1882, Henrik Ibsen, En folkefiende‎, page 162:
          hundene, som vi mennesker er så overmåde nær i slægt med
          The dogs, to which we humans are so exceedingly closely related.
        • 1888, Henrik Ibsen, Fruen fra havet‎, page 219:
          i den yderste nød og fare vover vi læger så meget
          In the most desperate need and danger, we doctors dare so much.
        • 1919, Nils Collett Vogt, Digte i utvalg‎, page 22:
          det var vi, som blev stedbørn paa jord
          It was we who became stepchildren on earth.
        • 1922, Nils Kjær, Samlede Skrifter‎, volume III: Profiler, page 263:
          vi unge, vi som endnu er saa passelig unge
          We young people, we who are still reasonably young.
        • 1926, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, “En ungdom, som er stærk og sund”, in Francis Bull, editor, Samlede Digte‎, volume II, page 169:
          en ungdom som er stærk og sund, er alt, vi ævner, én gang til
          A strong and healthy younger generation is everything we are capable of, once again.
        • 1929, Bergens Aftenblad, number 240, page 3, columns 5–6:
          dessuten fører vi endel smukke imitationer, som har en forbløffende likhet med skindhansker
          Furthermore, we carry some handsome imitations that bear a striking resemblance to leather gloves.
        • 1945 May 7, Knut Hamsun, “Adolf Hitler”, in Aftenposten‎, number 208, page 1, column 7:
          Og vi, hans nære Tilhengere, bøier nu vaare Hoder ved hans Død.
          And we, his close followers, now bow our heads at his death.
        • 2005, Inge Eidsvåg, Den gode lærer i liv og diktning‎:
          som lærere bør vi la oss inspirere av både Sokrates og Jesus
          As teachers, we should allow ourselves to be inspired by both Socrates and Jesus.
      3. (generalizing) we, one; people in general, including the speaker[2]
        Vi kan ikke vite hva fremtiden bringer. ― We cannot know what the future holds.
      4. we, I; used by a single speaker or writer when presenting an argument, describing a scene or considering what to do, sometimes including the audience
        I neste kapittel skal vi undersøke årsakene nærmere. ― In the next chapter, we will examine the causes more closely.
        nå skal vi se — let's see; used when pausing to think, recall something or decide what to do
        Nå skal vi se, hvor la jeg nøklene? ― Let's see, where did I put the keys?
        • 1883, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, “Over ævne, første stykke, Anden handling”, in Samlede digter-verker‎, volume V, published 1919, page 132:
          Døren er vid-åpen. Vi ser ut i et trangt landskap.
          The door is wide open. We look out onto a confined landscape.
        • 1922, Nils Kjær, Samlede Skrifter‎, volume III: Profiler, page 117:
          tænk Dem, at vi sidder i teatret og ser Den stundesløse
          Imagine that we are sitting in the theatre watching The Fussy Man.
        • 2015, Endre Mørck, “Hovedtrekk ved akkusativ med infinitiv i mellomnorsk”, in Maal og Minne‎, number 2, page 46:
          Vi skal i denne artikkelen ta for oss omfanget av bruken av akkusativ med infinitiv i mellomnorsk […]
          In this article, we will examine the extent of the use of the accusative with infinitive in Middle Norwegian […].
      5. (solemn, sometimes humorous) we, I; used by a monarch or another person speaking as though possessing exalted authority
        Vi har besluttet å benåde fangen. ― We have decided to pardon the prisoner.
        vi alene vide — literally “we alone know”; a formula associated with absolute authority or an arrogant claim to know best
        The expression preserves an obsolete plural verb form. It alludes to a reply issued by Frederik VI in 1835 concerning freedom of the press.[4]
        Svaret fra ledelsen var preget av holdningen «vi alene vide». ― Management's reply reflected a “we know best” attitude.
        • 1833 January 8, Henrik Wergeland, “Om Norges Selvstændighedstegn”, in Herman Jæger and Didrik Arup Seip, editor, Samlede Skrifter: trykt og utrykt‎, volume III,1, published 1932, page 420:
          Vi Norges grundlovmæssige Konge Carl den IIden Johan, Konge til Sverige, de Gothers og Venders, o. s. v.
          We, Norway's constitutional King Charles II John, King of Sweden, of the Goths and Wends, etc.
        • 1861, Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson, “Kong Sverre”, in Samlede digter-verker‎, volume II, published 1919, page 69:
          Vi takker dig for saa frivilligt tilbud.
          We thank you for such a freely made offer.
      6. you; used in sympathetic, coaxing, patronizing or joking address, especially to a child or patient
        Har vi sovet godt i natt? ― Have you slept well tonight?
        • 1891, Gabriel Finne, To Damer‎, page 39:
          er vi endda sån’t et stort barn, hva?
          Are we still such a big child, then?
        • 1900, Vilhelm Krag, Isaac Seehuusen‎, page 56:
          ei, ei lille jomfru, hvilken yndig kaabe vi dog har paa i aften
          Well, well, young miss, what a lovely cloak we are wearing this evening.
        • 1917, Gunnar Heiberg, Samlede dramatiske verker‎, volume I, page 213:
          hvordan har vi det saa idag?
          And how are we today?
        • 1925, Vilhelm Krag, Baldevin‎, page 123:
          er det noget vi har paa samvittigheden?
          Is there something on our conscience?
      Usage notes
      • Vi is the subject form. The object form is oss, which is also used reflexively: Vi vasker oss (“We wash ourselves”).
      • The possessive forms are vår, vårt and våre.
      • In ordinary plural use, vi can include or exclude the person being addressed; the distinction depends on context.
      • The pronoun can be followed by a numeral or a noun identifying the group, as in vi to (“the two of us”) and vi lærere (“we teachers”).
      • Use directed at another person can express warmth or solidarity, but may also sound patronizing.
      Related terms
      • oss (“us; ourselves”)
      • vår (“our; ours”)
      • vårt (“our; ours (neuter singular)”)
      • våre (“our; ours (plural)”)

      Etymology 2

      Nominalization of vi (“we”).

      Noun

      vi n (definite singular vi-et)

      1. a we; a group understood as a united whole, or a shared collective identity
        Gjennom samarbeidet ble de et vi. ― Through working together, they became a united group.
        • 2017, Stig Aasvik, Lofotveggen, page 129:
          føde et ventende barn, gifte seg, skape seg et hjem, et vi
          Give birth to an expected child, get married, make oneself a home, a we.
        • 2026 August 29, Klassekampen, page 2:
          vi-et favner om alle som lever i dette landet
          The collective we embraces everyone living in this country.
      2. the royal we
        Kongen brukte det kongelige vi. ― The king used the royal we.
        • 2004, Susanne Agerholm, Liv laga‎:
          Vi. Det kongelige vi

      3. the editorial we

      Sassarese

      Alternative forms

      Etymology

      From Latin ibi (“there; then”), from Proto-Italic *iðei or *ifei with iambic shortening, from the pronominal stem Proto-Indo-European *éy.

      Adverb

      vi

      1. here
        Synonym: zi
        1. in or at this place
        2. to or into this place
      2. there
        Synonym: zi
        1. in or at that place
          • 1866 [1770s], Antonio Martini, chapter XVII, in Giovanni Spano, transl., L'ebagneliu sigundu S. Matteju [The Gospel according to St. Matthew]‎, London, verse 26, page 68, translation of Il santo Vangelo di Gesù Cristo secondo Matteo (in Italian):
            Ma pa no ilcandalizzalli, vai a mari, e getta l’amu: e piglia lu primu pesciu, chi n’alzarà: e abbrendili la bocca v’hai a incuntrà un iltateri: pigliannilu, e paga pal me, e pal te.
            But, so as to not cause them indignation, go to the sea, and cast the hook; and take the first fish that comes up; and, opening its mouth, there you will find a stater; take it, and pay for me, and for yourself.
          • 1989, Giovanni Maria Cherchi, “Ulisse [Ulysses]”, in La poesia di l'althri [The poetry of others] (overall work in Italian and Sassarese), Sassari: Arnoldo Mondadori Editore, page 51:
            Raramenti vi fàrani pizoni,
            si sò abbramiddi, pa’ zirchà ricattu.
            Birds seldom glide there, if they are hungry, to look for food.
        2. to or into that place
          • 1866 [1770s], Antonio Martini, chapter XXI, in Giovanni Spano, transl., L'ebagneliu sigundu S. Matteju [The Gospel according to St. Matthew]‎, London, verse 29, page 84, translation of Il santo Vangelo di Gesù Cristo secondo Matteo (in Italian):
            Ma eddu rilpundendi, dizisi: No v’ andu. Ma poi, pintiddu, v’ andesi.
            But he, answering, said: "I will not go there". But afterwards, regretful, he went there.

      Pronoun

      vi

      1. (accusative) you (plural)
        • 1866 [1770s], Antonio Martini, chapter IV, in Giovanni Spano, transl., L'ebagneliu sigundu S. Matteju [The Gospel according to St. Matthew]‎, London, verse 19, page 11, translation of Il santo Vangelo di Gesù Cristo secondo Matteo (in Italian):
          E li dizisi: Viniddi dareddu a me, e vi aggiu a fà pilcadori d’ omini.
          And he said to them: "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.
        • 1989, Giovanni Maria Cherchi, “Puisia [Poem]”, in La poesia di l'althri [The poetry of others] (overall work in Italian and Sassarese), Sassari: Arnoldo Mondadori Editore, page 19:
          […] un’oasi prupizia pa’ pudé / cu lu pientu annittavvi da li fàuri / chi vi sò già incighendi.
          A propitious oasis, so I can cleanse you with my tears from the lies that are already blinding you.
      2. (dative) to you (plural)
        Abà vi diggu la veriddai ― I'll tell you the truth now (literally, “Now to you I tell the truth”)
        • 1866 [1770s], Antonio Martini, translated by Giovanni Spano, L'ebagneliu sigundu S. Matteju [The Gospel according to St. Matthew]‎, London, verse 18, page 14, translation of Il santo Vangelo di Gesù Cristo secondo Matteo (in Italian):
          Palchì vi diggu in viriddai; finza chi passia lu zelu e la terra, no ha a vinì mancu un etti, o un puntu di la leggi finza chi tuttu si cumplia.
          for truly I say to you, until the heaven and the earth may pass away, one iota or one tittle may not pass away from the Law, until all may come to pass

      Serbo-Croatian

      Etymology

      Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vy.

      Pronunciation

      • IPA(key): /ʋîː/

      Pronoun

      vȋ ? (Cyrillic spelling ви̑)

      1. you (nominative plural of tȋ (“you”))
      2. you (vocative plural of tȋ (“you”))
      3. (regional, Montenegro, Torlakian) you (clitic dative plural of tȋ (“you”))
      4. (formal) you (formal singular and plural)

      Usage notes

      The clitic dative forms in the plural correspond to the Old Church Slavonic вꙑ (vy) and Old Church Slavonic нꙑ (ny). However, it has primarily been attested in rural areas, most notably across Montenegro, where it has been preserved and is still in use. Cognates include Bulgarian ви (vi) and Bulgarian ни (ni), where it has been preserved even in the accusative case.

      Swedish

      Pronunciation

      • IPA(key): /viː/
      • Audio (Gotland):(file)
      • Rhymes: -iː

      Etymology 1

      From Old Swedish vīr, from Old East Norse *wīʀ (compare vér), from Proto-Germanic *wīz, from Proto-Indo-European *wéy, plural of *éǵh₂.

      Pronoun

      vi

      1. we (first-person personal plural subject pronoun)
        • 1791, Carl Michael Bellman, Fredmans sånger, N:o 21
          Så lunka vi så småningom från Bacchi buller och tumult
          We'll walk away eventually from the noise and tumult of Bacchus
        • 1974, Lasse Tennander, “Ska vi gå hem till dig [Shall We Go to Your Place ["home to you" – idiomatic]]”, in Allting som ni gör kan jag göra bättre [Anything You Do, I Can Do Better [a cover album]]‎, performed by Magnus Uggla:
          Ska vi gå hem till dig eller hem till mig, eller var och en hem till sitt? Ska vi göra som dom andra och ägna oss åt varandra, eller ska var och en sköta sitt?
          Shall we go to your place ["home to you" – idiomatic] or to my place [home to me], or each one ["each and one" – idiomatic] home to theirs [nominalized – neuter gender is used when there is no concrete referent, like in impersonal constructions and here, as a rule of thumb]? Shall we do like the others and spend time on each other [engage in each other as an activity – doesn't have the connotations of "devote"], or shall each one mind [take care of] theirs [nominalized]?
        • 1981, X Models, “Två av oss [Two of us]”‎:
          Det finns bara en av mig och det är jag. Det finns bara en av dig och det är du. Det finns bara två av oss, och det är vi.
          There is only one of me and that is I. There is only one of you [object] and that is you [subject]. There are only two of us, and that is us [we – subject]. [Swedish has some of the same subject/object fuzziness as English, but a standalone "Det är <pronoun>" idiomatically (through intuition rather than being taught) uses the subject form]
      Usage notes

      A standalone "That is us" is idiomatically "Det är vi" rather than "Det är oss." Compare "That is I" in (taught) English, which also uses the subject form. See the quotations above for an example.

      Etymology 2

      From Old Swedish hvi, from Old Norse hví, from Proto-Germanic *hwī (“by what, how”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷey, locative of *kʷís (“who”). Cognate with Old Danish hvi, Danish hvi, Old West Norse hví, Norwegian Nynorsk kvi, Norwegian Bokmål hvi, Old Saxon hwi, hwiu, Old High German hwiu, Middle High German wiu, German wie (“how”), Old English hwȳ, hwī, Middle English why, English why, more distantly with Latin quī (“what, who, which”).

        • 1541, Gustav Vasa Bible, Matthew 9:4
          Men när Jesus sågh theras tanckar, sadhe han, Hwj tencken j ondt j idhor hierta?

          And Jesus knowing their thoughts said, Wherefore think ye evil in your hearts?
        Synonym: varför
